AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: We report our experience with metabolic syndrome screening for obese living kidney donor candidates to mitigate the long-term risk of CKD.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: We retrospectively reviewed 814 obese (BMI≥30) and 993 nonobese living kidney donor evaluations over 12 years. Using logistic regression, we explored interactions between social/clinical variables and candidate acceptance before and after policy implementation.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Obese donor candidate acceptance decreased after metabolic syndrome screening began (56.3%, 46.3%, p < 0.01), while nonobese candidate acceptance remained similar (59.6%, 59.2%, p = 0.59). Adjusting for age, gender, race, BMI, and number of prior evaluations, acceptance of obese candidates decreased significantly more than nonobese (p = 0.025). In candidates without metabolic syndrome, there was no significant change in how age, sex, race, or BMI affected a donor candidate's probability of acceptance.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: Metabolic syndrome screening is a simple stratification tool for centers with liberal absolute BMI cut-offs to exclude potentially higher-risk obese candidates.

AbstractText.Label: SUMMARY
AbstractText.content: Our center screens obese living kidney donor candidates for metabolic syndrome to maximize donation opportunities while excluding a potentially higher-risk population of mild and moderately obese donor candidates. Retrospective review of 814 obese (BMI≥30) and 993 nonobese living kidney donor evaluations over 12 years found this policy decreased donor acceptance rate without introducing new age, gender or racial biases.
